items.q: Is there a Swiss golden visa?
items.a: Not in the sense of buying residence through an investment. Switzerland does offer routes for people who move without working here, for example as a financially independent person or a retiree, and these are assessed by the canton case by case.

items.q: Do I need to work in Switzerland to live here?
items.a: No. Many of the families we help do not take up work in Switzerland. The right route depends mainly on your citizenship, your plans and your circumstances.

items.q: How long does the process take?
items.a: It depends on your route and on the canton. After a first conversation we give you a realistic timeline, including what can be prepared before you move.

howItWorks.description: From the first question to your first year in Switzerland: how we guide families through permits, tax, the choice of canton and settling in.
howItWorks.intro: Moving country is a big decision. We break it into clear steps and stay with you throughout, so you always know what comes next.

steps.title: A first conversation

result.disclaimer: This is a general indication based on your answers, not legal or tax advice. Permits and lump-sum taxation are decided by the cantonal authorities case by case.

R0.label: Swiss citizen
R0.text: You do not need a permit. Lump-sum taxation is not available to Swiss nationals, so ordinary taxation applies.

R1_NONE.label: EU/EFTA free movement, without work
R1_NONE.text: A B permit without gainful activity, provided you have sufficient means and Swiss health insurance.

R1_ACTIVE.label: EU/EFTA free movement, with work
R1_ACTIVE.text: A B permit based on employment or self-employment in Switzerland.

R1_UNSURE.label: EU/EFTA free movement
R1_UNSURE.text: A B permit, either without gainful activity (with sufficient means and Swiss health insurance) or based on work in Switzerland. We will look at which fits your plans.

R2.label: Non-EU, working in Switzerland
R2.text: A work permit subject to quotas. The UK has its own quota; other countries fall under the third-country quotas, which are restrictive. This route is driven by an employer or a business plan.

R3.label: Non-EU, retiree
R3.text: Residence for people aged 55 or over who no longer work, in Switzerland or abroad (Art. 28 AIG); managing your own assets is allowed. It requires special personal ties to Switzerland (owning property is not enough) and sufficient means for life. The canton decides at its discretion and the SEM must approve. It is often combined with the fiscal-interest route.

R4.label: Non-EU, important fiscal interest
R4.text: A discretionary permit for an important fiscal interest (Art. 30 para. 1 lit. b AIG): the canton proposes it and the SEM must approve. It usually goes with lump-sum taxation at a level the canton sets (Geneva, for example, publishes CHF 750,000 as its expenditure base for this route). A tax agreement alone is not a permit.

MAY_BE_ELIGIBLE.label: May be eligible
MAY_BE_ELIGIBLE.text: From your answers, lump-sum taxation (based on your living expenses) may be an option. Whether it is worthwhile depends on your income, your assets and the canton.

UNLIKELY.label: Unlikely to be efficient
UNLIKELY.text: Your spending level appears to be below the federal minimum base, so ordinary taxation is probably the better fit.

NOT_AVAILABLE.label: Not available
NOT_AVAILABLE.text: Lump-sum taxation is not open to Swiss nationals, to people who work in Switzerland, or to people who were tax-resident in Switzerland in the last ten years (unless they were taxed on a lump sum then). Ordinary taxation applies.

TO_ASSESS.label: To be assessed
TO_ASSESS.text: We need a little more information to tell whether lump-sum taxation is relevant for you. If you were taxed on a lump sum in Switzerland before, you may be able to use it again.

lumpSum.coupleNote: For married couples, under current law both spouses must meet the conditions. We confirm the position for your household with the canton.
lumpSum.r4Flag: For non-EU nationals not working in Switzerland, residence is usually linked to lump-sum taxation. We would need to discuss your situation.

flags.UK: UK: the remittance basis was abolished from 6 April 2025 (four-year FIG regime, and a Temporary Repatriation Facility for earlier foreign income and gains); long-term UK residents (10 of the last 20 tax years) can remain liable to UK inheritance tax on worldwide assets for 3 to 10 years after leaving; for British nationals who plan to work, the UK permit quota.
flags.FR: France: the France–Switzerland treaty has special rules for lump-sum taxpayers; confirm your position in a tax ruling before moving. French exit tax on unrealised gains (art. 167 bis CGI).
flags.DE: Germany: exit taxation (§ 6 AStG) on holdings of 1% or more if you were fully taxable in Germany for at least 7 of the last 12 years; a modified lump sum for German-source income.
flags.MODIFIED: A modified lump sum is needed to claim treaty benefits on income from your current country.
flags.US_CITIZEN: US citizens remain taxable in the United States, so the benefit of a lump sum may be limited. Swiss banks also apply FATCA onboarding rules.
flags.PLAN_EARLY: Plan the change of tax residence and your bank and KYC documentation early. Your current country may also have its own exit or tax rules.
flags.PLAN_EARLY_NON_EU: Plan the change of tax residence and your bank and KYC documentation early. Your current country may also have its own exit or tax rules. Without Swiss or EU/EFTA citizenship, the non-EU permit routes apply.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.description: How Switzerland Residency handles your personal data: contact form, eligibility check, analytics and your rights.

p: This website is operated by Ark Fiduciaire SA, Geneva, Switzerland, under the name Switzerland Residency. We are responsible for the processing of personal data described here, under the Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection (FADP) and, where it applies, the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
For any question about your data, write to us via the [contact form](/en/contact/) on this website.

When you send us a message, we receive your name, email address, optional phone number, preferred language, your message and, if you choose to include it, your eligibility check result. We use this information only to answer your request and, if you wish, to prepare a proposal.
Form submissions are transmitted through Formspark, a form processing service. If you contact us by WhatsApp, WhatsApp also processes your message.

The eligibility check runs entirely in your browser. Your answers are not sent to us or to anyone else. If you choose to pass your result to the contact form, it is kept temporarily in your browser's session storage and deleted when you close the tab.

With your consent, we use Google Analytics 4 to understand how the site is used, for example which pages are read and whether the eligibility check is completed. Without your consent, Google Analytics is not loaded and no analytics cookies are set.
We never send the content of your answers or messages to Google Analytics. You can change your choice at any time through the cookie settings link at the bottom of every page.
We keep your messages for as long as needed to answer you and, if we work together, for the periods required by Swiss law. Analytics data is kept for a limited period set in Google Analytics.

You can ask to see, correct or delete your personal data, and object to its processing, by writing to us via the [contact form](/en/contact/) on this website. You may also contact the Swiss Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC) or your local supervisory authority.
